description.p: Solarxy is a cross-platform 3D model viewer and validator built in Rust with wgpu. It loads OBJ, STL, PLY, and glTF/GLB models and renders them with real-time PBR shading (Cook-Torrance, IBL, SSAO, bloom).

ul.li: Real-time PBR rendering with HDRI image-based lighting
Inspection modes: shaded, material ID, UV map, texel density, depth
Material overrides (clay, chrome, silhouette) for shape evaluation
Split viewport with independent or linked cameras
Validation overlay: degenerate triangles, missing UVs, normal mismatches
Companion CLI (solarxy-cli) for scripted analysis and CI integration

description.p: Path-traced rendering. A second renderer joins the real-time one: a physically based GPU path tracer that renders converged stills with global illumination, soft shadows from every light, real depth of field, and the camera's own colour grade, tiled to eight thousand pixels an edge. A per-pane preview converges in the viewport, and a new render command makes the terminal a first-class host: scene file in, PNG or floating-point EXR out with albedo, normal and depth passes, deterministic under a fixed seed, with progress on a plain line, a dashboard, or a live window.

Rendering foundations: five things the renderer got wrong, closed together. Imported materials keep their glass and their coatings through a widened principled surface. The HDRI a scene is lit with now saves inside it. Instanced scatters render without allocating a real copy per instance. Colour grading arrives, owned by the camera, with exposure, tone mapping, lift, gamma and gain, and grading tables in Adobe cube format. Light intensity becomes physical.

A scene stops being a static arrangement of settings and starts being something that computes, moves, and can leave the editor. Any numeric parameter can hold a formula that reads other nodes and measures its own geometry; the attribute wrangle takes the same language to a single point; a timeline drives time-varying scenes; and rect-area lights land alongside publishing improvements.

The first modeling wave. Geometry carries named attributes on points and primitives, the registry grows from 58 to 74 node types, and the viewport draws point clouds and polylines. Scatter points over any surface, stamp copies onto them, randomize a colour per point, and inspect every value in the new attributes pane.
A polish and bug-fix pass across the web app and the desktop viewer.

Typed node contexts take the web app's catalogue from 33 to 58 node types: dedicated material and texture networks, camera nodes any pane can look through, turntable export, and file export to OBJ, STL, PLY and GLB. Every node, port and parameter is now documented in the app and in the generated node reference, and a first-run tour introduces the interface.

The desktop app adopts the unified design language: one palette now drives the desktop GUI, the web app and the analyze TUI from a single definition. The themes are now named Dark and Light (existing preference files migrate automatically), the light theme is the warm koljam.com palette, and the console, hover states and error screens were fixed for the light ground.

Solarxy Web: the viewer, validator and review toolset arrive in the browser on WebGPU, with node-based parametric modelling on a shared Rust core. 33 node types, typed ports, subflows, transform gizmos, a dockable workspace, textures and materials, and the self-contained .slxy scene format (schema frozen at version 1).
Desktop gains the renderer work the web shell required: a multi-object scene path, mip-mapped texture filtering, correct base-colour factors on untextured materials, and a generalised light array.

A review and annotation system arrives: enter review mode, drop categorised markers on the model itself, reply, resolve and re-anchor, all saved in a sidecar file the whole team can read. Panels become dockable with persistent layouts, a Material Inspector introspects textures and PBR values, overdraw and ambient-occlusion preview join the inspection modes, and batch validation gains adapters for continuous-integration pipelines.

Solarxy splits into two binaries, the GUI viewer and a terminal companion, each with native install channels per platform. Preferences move from the terminal into a tabbed in-app dialog, and a complete interface surface lands: menu bar, console, toast notifications, an update modal and a keyboard-shortcuts overlay.

Packaging rearchitecture: GUI binary now ships as a true Windows-subsystem app (no console flicker on Start Menu launch), Linux GUI moves to Flatpak (this build), CLI splits into a separate solarxy-cli binary distributable via Homebrew tap, and macOS adds a Homebrew Cask path for one-step install with automatic Gatekeeper bypass.
